_note: Written by Sumukh (questions are his exact wording). 'expected' and paper locations filled in by Claude from the paper text, for grading. answerable: true / false / 'partial' / 'near-miss'.

questions.q: how many sentence pairs were there in english german dataset wmt 2014?
what averaging technique does smoothing module apply?
questions.expected: An exponential moving average (EMA): z_bar_t = P_t * z_hat_t + (1 - P_t) * z_bar_{t-1}. [Dynamic Chunking §2.2.2 p.7]

questions.q: what do spectron and PSLM use as prefix to generating speech?
questions.expected: Text: they first produce the utterance as text tokens, then use them as a prefix to generate speech ('Chain-of-Modality'). [Moshi §2 p.5]

questions.q: what is used To discretize waveforms into audio tokens?
questions.expected: Mimi, a neural audio codec, using residual vector quantization (RVQ). [Moshi §3.3 p.9]. Names no paper: tests unnamed-paper retrieval.

Moshi/Helium pre-training data: a fastText classifier (9 categories, trained on high-quality sources vs random CommonCrawl), applied per line, averaged weighted by line length, documents kept above a threshold. [Moshi §3.2.2 p.8-9]. Names no paper.

questions.q: why Alternate Language Datasets are also explored Besides conventional language modeling? what all alternatives were explored?
questions.expected: Chinese, code and DNA, because each challenges tokenization: Chinese has 3-byte characters and no spaces; code has lots of whitespace and latent hierarchy; DNA has no natural tokenization cues. [Dynamic Chunking §3.2 p.15]. Two-part question: both parts needed for 'correct'.

questions.q: how does HNet compare with Mixture of experts?
questions.expected: H-Net can be seen as dynamic sparsity like MoE (more parameters, same FLOPs), but it beats a FLOPs-matched byte-level MoE (LlamaByte-MoE), so its gains are not just from sparsity. [Dynamic Chunking §3.3 p.19-20]
The model has no recurrence and no convolution, so information about token order/position must be injected. [Transformer §3.5 p.6]

questions.q: can i use batch norm instead of layer norm?
questions.expected: Near miss: the Transformer uses layer normalization (LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))) [Transformer §3.1 p.3], but none of the papers discusses or tests batch norm. Correct = say what is used and that the papers don't answer the swap question. Wrong = any claim that batch norm would or wouldn't work.

questions.q: what is the core difference between encoder and decoder in transformer architecture.
questions.expected: Both are stacks of N=6 layers. The decoder adds a third sub-layer doing multi-head attention over the encoder's output, and masks its self-attention so a position can't attend to later positions (auto-regressive). [Transformer §3.1 p.3]

questions.q: what role does self attention play in modelling conversational context in moshi?
questions.expected: Partial: Moshi describes a Temporal Transformer (initialised from Helium) modelling minutes of context over multi-stream audio + text tokens, but never explicitly states 'the role of self-attention in conversational context'. Correct = stated facts with citations and an honest note on what isn't said. Wrong = unsupported explanation.

questions.q: dynamic chunking reduces unnecessary context by learning boundaries and compressing the sequences. could a similar mechanism work to reduce moshi's computational overhead?
questions.expected: Speculative cross-paper: neither paper evaluates dynamic chunking for Moshi. Correct = describe what dynamic chunking does (learned boundaries, compression into chunks) and what Moshi does about its own cost (e.g. low 12.5 Hz frame rate, RQ-Transformer splitting time and depth), with citations, and say the papers don't test the combination. Wrong = a confident yes/no.

Not answerable: DeepSeek appears only as a citation (learning-rate schedules with long constant phases) [Dynamic Chunking §4 p.23]. The papers don't say what it does differently. Must refuse (may mention it's only cited).
Not answerable: 'JEV' appears in none of the papers. Must refuse, without using outside knowledge.

Answerable from the papers, narrowly: floating point operations, used to measure training cost. The Transformer estimates them as training time x number of GPUs x sustained single-precision capacity per GPU [Transformer §6.1, Table 2 footnote]; Dynamic Chunking uses FLOPs to match compute budgets across models [Dynamic Chunking §3 p.11]. Tests 'answer from the papers, not from memory'.
